reasons: Only the night-word is cognate (ON nætr ~ Gk νύξ ~ Lat. noctes ~ Ved. náktam < *nókʷt-); the day-word differs in every branch, so the shared material is one lexeme in a near-universal time merism. Among the anchors only the ON one (Þiðreks saga, a translated text: riðr with nætr and ðaga, night first, adverbial accusative) has the claimed form. Plato is a day-first nominative list of time-divisions (ἡμέρα, νὺξ); Galen/Damocrates is a measured soaking interval (νύκτα, then one ἡμέραν). The Irish (Eochair-Sgiath an Aifrinn, 1898 devotional prose) is day-first (ló before oidhche), both words non-cognate and plausibly modelled on the Latin day-first formula (die, nocte), so it is no witness. The night-first plural pattern in Homer (νύκτας with ἦμαρ), Ennius/Lucretius (noctes with dies) and ON saga prose (nætr with daga) is a real and somewhat marked agreement, possibly tied to reckoning by nights, but parallel development in a universal merism cannot be excluded, and Vedic usually puts dívā first. A defensible lead, not compelling. (Only the Irish anchor was opened in its corpus; the ON, Greek and Latin texts were read as given in the claim.)

Passage verified (TBC LL, O'Rahilly 1967, lines 29-32: darochratar, formna, bó, fer, ech, slaidius). bó ~ go-, fer ~ vīra-, ech ~ aśva- are exact cognates, but they are the ordinary words for cow, man and horse in both languages, so any list of a pastoral community's living wealth comes out 'cognate'. The claim overstates the match. The order is not the same: Irish cow-man-horse; AVŚ 1.16.4 cow-horse-man; AVŚ 12.2.29 horse-man-cow-goat-sheep; RV 1.114.8 cow-horse, then men. The main AV anchor fills the man slot with pūruṣa-, not vīra- (vīra- appears only in the compound avīrahā). AVŚ 12.2.29 adds goats and sheep, so it is an open livestock list. The Windisch TBC support is the same LL text, not an independent witness. In the Celtic layer the triad is a one-off (other fer/ech hits are the 'breaths of men and horses'). The congruence of 'living wealth slain' is real, and men+cattle is a recognised IE merism, but the Irish has no *peḱu- and the triad is natural. Plausible, not compelling.

Both members are exact cognates: Ved. r̥tá- = Av. aṣ̌a- (PIIr *Hr̥tá-), Ved. drúh-/druhvan- = Av. druj- (PIIr *drugʰ-), with r̥tā́van- = aṣ̌auuan- as a suffixal equation. The anchors themselves are only loosely congruent: ṛtāvṛdhau gods repel the druhvāṇaṃ (nudethe), and Sraoša aṣ̌iiō questions the drujim (apərəsat̰), with unrelated verbs. But the corpora confirm a genuine shared collocation, verified in VedaWeb and CAB: truth in the instrumental or dative as means or ally, with the druh as object of a verb of overcoming. Vedic: RV 1.133.1 r̥téna with drúhas and dahāmi; RV 7.75.1 r̥téna with drúhas and āvar; RV 2.23.17 druhó with hantā́ and r̥tásya. Avestan: Y48.1 aṣ̌ā with drujim and və̄ṇghaitī; Y30.8 aṣ̌āi with zastaiiō and drujim. The Avestan dualist systematisation is a drift. The Gathic attestation and the Vedic common-noun usage in the same frame make borrowing or chance unlikely, and the words are culture-specific religious terms, not a generic phrase. Accepted as Proto-Indo-Iranian phraseology, not deeper PIE.

Irish passage verified: Regimen na Sláinte, the Irish translation of Magninus Mediolanensis' Regimen sanitatis (cosa, nigi, huisgi, fhuar). It presumably renders a Latin instruction to wash the feet in cold water and is derivative (the edition title alone establishes the translation). The Greek anchors are NT John 13 and texts dependent on it or on the same hospitality topos (Origen, Testament of Abraham, Vita Aesopi). nigid ~ νίζω/νίπτω (*neygʷ-/*nigʷ-) is a correct cognate pair, but nigid is the ordinary Irish verb for washing. cos is not cognate with πούς. uisce shares only the root with ὕδωρ (a different formation) and is construed differently (Irish a + dative; Greek object of βάλλω). 'Wash the feet with water' is a universal practical phrase, and the claim's own residue (the verb's semantic range for washing the extremities) is lexical semantics, not phraseology. (Greek anchors read as given in the claim, not reopened in GLAUx.)

The etymologies are right (OIr. tír < *tīros- ~ Lat. terra < *ters-, Matasović; muir ~ mare < *mori-). But these are the ordinary words for land and sea in both languages, so a land-and-sea merism comes out cognate automatically, and 'by land and sea' is a near-universal pairing. The anchors do not show the formula. Keating (G100054, 1902-14 ed.) is literal, an army by land (thír) and an army by sea (mhuir). Plautus Amph. 1055 is a cosmic triad (mare, terra, caelum). Lucretius 6.633 is physical description (mare, terris). The order differs: Irish usually puts muir first, Latin terra. The Irish annal usage was written by Latin-literate clerics and the Welsh Brut is translated from Latin, so both are exposed to the Latin formula (terra, marique). Generic and possibly calqued. (Latin anchors read as given in the claim, not reopened in LASLA.)

Passage verified (Stair Nuadat Find Femin, ed. 1921: doruc, ingin, tuccad, Sláine, ainm, fuire). ainm ~ ὄνομα (*h₁nómn̥) is exact, and Herodotus 4.10 (οὐνόματα with θέσθαι) is a genuine *h₁nómn̥ dʰeh₁- witness, as are Greek and Vedic nā́ma with dhā-. But the Irish anchor contributes only the noun. Its verb is 'give' (tuccad), the generic way to say 'give a name' in many languages, and the 'name on X' frame (for + pronoun) is also the Latin impose-a-name type (nomen with imponere). The Irish stock phrase (tuccad, ainm, fair) clusters in saints' lives right after baptism and in translated romances, a context exposed to Latin. The MW dodi witness would help only if dodi < *dʰeh₁- were secure, which the claim itself declines to assert. A real inherited collocation in Greek and Indo-Iranian, but weak as a Celtic continuation. (Herodotus read as given in the claim, not reopened in GLAUx.)

Both cognations hold: MW clun < *klowni- ~ Av. sraoni-, Skt. śróṇi-, Lat. clūnis; MW llydan < *litano- < *pl̥th₂- ~ Av. pərəθu- (Matasović). YtWay12.13f pərəϑu.sraōniš is verified in CAB. But the Welsh is not an epithet. In Peredur's description of the Loathly Damsel it is a predicative clause (glun, llydan, then an OCR-damaged adjective, probably 'bony') in a grotesque head-to-foot catalogue. The Avestan is a compound epithet of the male god Vayu in a list of epithets. 'Broad hips' is the obvious way to describe hips in any language, and both words are the default lexemes; the 'inverted beauty epithet' argument is special pleading. Context not comparable; a one-off in Welsh; coincidence.

Passage verified (Meyer, Irish Quatrains, a riding charm: Cros, Colmain, fitir, feba, ech). The roots are right: ro-fitir < *weyd-; feb < *wesu-/*weswā (Matasović); ech ~ aśva-. But the collocations are not congruent. The Irish means 'knows the excellences of horses': perfect-present 'know', abstract feb, horses in the genitive. Vedic vasuvíd- means 'finding goods', a stock epithet of many gods with nothing to do with horses, and the horses appear only in a simile (aśvāḥ drawing a chariot). Different meanings, different syntax, the horse in a different role, and the Irish is a single late Christian quatrain. A chance meeting of common roots, as the claim itself concedes.
